subject: religious-studies

moments.title: Luther's 95 Theses
moments.who: Martin Luther, Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg
moments.body: On 31 October 1517, Luther posts (or sends — the door-posting is contested) 95 theses for academic disputation, attacking the sale of indulgences by Johann Tetzel. The Theses, in Latin, are translated into German and printed within months. The Reformation begins.

quote.text: Here I stand, I can do no other.
quote.attrib: Luther, reportedly at the Diet of Worms, 1521

moments.takeaway: Without the printing press (Gutenberg, c. 1440) Luther's protest would have been local. With it, his pamphlets reached enormous audiences within months.

moments.title: The Act of Supremacy
moments.body: Henry VIII, refused an annulment by Rome, declares himself Supreme Head of the Church of England. The English Reformation is initially political and dynastic; doctrinal reform follows under Edward VI (1547-1553), reverses under Mary I (1553-1558), and consolidates under Elizabeth I (1558-1603).
moments.takeaway: The Reformation in England was driven by Henry's dynastic crisis as much as by theology. The Elizabethan Settlement is a compromise still visible in the Church of England today.

moments.title: Peace of Westphalia
moments.who: European powers ending the Thirty Years' War
moments.body: The wars of religion that followed the Reformation ended in 1648 with a treaty system that, broadly, accepted confessional diversity and the right of rulers to determine their states' religion (cuius regio, eius religio). It also marks the conventional birth of the modern sovereign state system.
moments.takeaway: Religious toleration emerged from exhaustion, not principle. The political form (the territorial state) was the lasting legacy as much as the theology.

now.title: Five centuries on
now.body: Protestantism is now extremely diverse — Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Baptist, Pentecostal and many more. The 2017 Reformation 500 commemorations saw Pope Francis travel to Lund, Sweden, for a joint Catholic-Lutheran service — unthinkable a century earlier. The Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999) formally narrowed the original sola fide dispute.
now.open_questions: Was the Reformation the start of secular modernity? Charles Taylor's 'A Secular Age' (2007) argues yes — internalised religion, the disenchantment of nature and the rise of the individual conscience all have Reformation roots. Brad Gregory's 'The Unintended Reformation' (2012) is more critical.

reflection: A single Augustinian friar's protest against indulgences split Western Christendom, redrew political maps, and reshaped epistemology. The unintended consequences of doctrinal disputes can be civilisational.
